det_01.label: The Pudding's 2018 one-hit wonders article
det_01.content: This dataset accompanies The Pudding's April 2018 article 'One-Hit Wonders in Sports' by Russell Goldenberg and Jan Diehm. The piece asks a deceptively simple question: which professional athletes had exactly one great year, then disappeared? The authors looked at eight pro leagues over thirty years (1988–2017), ranked every player each season by a sport-appropriate statistic, and defined a 'one-hit wonder' as a player who finished in the top 20 exactly once and never came within striking distance (top 50) in any other season of their career. The result is both a statistical exercise in outliers and a human story about careers that never made it back.

det_02.label: What the ranking stat is for each sport
det_02.content: Each league uses a different single-number catch-all that approximates overall value. Basketball (NBA and WNBA) uses VORP — Value Over Replacement Player — a box-score estimate of a player's points above what a league-minimum replacement would produce. Baseball (MLB) uses WAR (Wins Above Replacement), hockey (NHL) uses point shares, tennis (ATP and WTA) uses year-end ranking points, and golf (PGA and LPGA) uses money earned on tour. These stats were chosen because they are the closest thing to apples-to-apples 'who was most valuable this season' within each sport, and because they have reasonably complete historical coverage back to the late 1980s. A consequence: 'top 20' means something slightly different sport-to-sport, but within a sport a top-20 season is unambiguously elite.

det_03.label: Why this is harder than it sounds: regression to the mean
det_03.content: Statisticians have a phrase for what makes a one-hit wonder story a one-hit wonder story: regression to the mean. When any measurement involves a mix of skill and luck — and a single sports season always does — the most extreme results in one year are disproportionately driven by lucky bounces, favorable matchups, or anomalously hot streaks. Next season, the skill remains but the luck resets, and the extreme outlier tends to drift back toward the crowd. In sports this is so common it has its own name, the 'sophomore slump,' and it produces the famous 'Sports Illustrated cover jinx': teams and players on the cover performed well enough to earn the spot, then performed more normally afterward. What The Pudding's dataset isolates is the extreme tail of this phenomenon: athletes whose one great year was so far above their baseline that they never again came close. These are not just sophomore slumps — they are careers where one season looks like a rounding error in the time series.

det_04.label: Dana Barros: the canonical NBA one-hit wonder
det_04.content: The poster child for the NBA in The Pudding's analysis is Dana Barros. In 1994–95, his second season with the Philadelphia 76ers, Barros averaged 20.6 points, 7.5 assists, and shot 46% from three over all 82 games. He won Most Improved Player, was voted an All-Star, and dropped a 50-point, 8-rebound night against the Houston Rockets. He also set an NBA record by hitting at least one three-pointer in 89 consecutive games. It was the only year of his 14-season career that he averaged even 14 points per game: his career average ended up at 10.5 PPG. Philadelphia could not keep him — Boston signed him to a big contract as a free agent — and his role immediately collapsed back to that of a rotational guard. His season rank in the NBA went from #8 at the peak to #153 in a typical year.

det_05.label: Dontrelle Willis: 'D-Train' and the collapse
det_05.content: Dontrelle Willis won NL Rookie of the Year for the 2003 Florida Marlins and helped them win the World Series, but it was his 2005 season — 22 wins, 2.63 ERA, five shutouts, the most wins in baseball — that made him the MLB's definitive one-hit wonder. He finished 2nd in Cy Young voting behind Chris Carpenter. The decline was swift and medically documented: after a trade to Detroit and the onset of what he later described as severe anxiety disorder, his control evaporated. His WAR went 6.5, 3.0, 0.9, and his rank tumbled from 8th in MLB to roughly 370th by the end of his career. Willis's story is the regression-to-the-mean chart reshaped by injury, mental health, and the specific pressure of being a 23-year-old face of a franchise.

det_06.label: Rich Beem: the PGA's unlikely major winner
det_06.content: Rich Beem sold car stereos and worked in a pro shop before his professional golf career took off. In August 2002 he won The International, then two weeks later won the PGA Championship at Hazeltine by holding off a charging Tiger Woods — Woods birdied his last four holes and still lost by one stroke. Beem briefly rose to #7 in the world. Within two years he was outside the top 180. In money-list terms he finished 4th on tour in 2002 and never again cracked the top 100. He is the perfect illustration of how a single four-day hot streak at one major can reshape a season's earnings and rank without reshaping the underlying golfer.

det_07.label: Jiri Hudler: the NHL pick
det_07.content: Jiri Hudler, a Czech winger who spent most of his career as a secondary scorer for Detroit and then Calgary, had one All-Star, Lady Byng-winning season in 2014–15 — 31 goals, 76 points, and a 13th-place finish in NHL point shares. His median career rank was 220. By 2017–18 he could not secure an NHL contract and soon retired. The NHL's deep roster talent and the role-player structure of the sport make hockey a particularly interesting one-hit-wonder case: Hudler was a legitimately good NHL player for a decade, but one season he was elite, and that year is a striking spike on his career timeline.

det_08.label: Women's leagues: WNBA, LPGA, WTA selections
det_08.content: The Pudding highlighted three women's-league one-hit wonders. Tracy Reid won 1998 WNBA Rookie of the Year with the Charlotte Sting, averaging 16.7 PPG, and her rank fell outside the top 100 the very next season. Hilary Lunke won the 2003 U.S. Women's Open in a Monday playoff — her only LPGA win — and never again finished in the LPGA money-list top 30. Karolina Sprem reached the 2004 Wimbledon quarterfinals and the WTA top 20, then spent the rest of her career outside the top 50 before retiring in 2008. Including women's leagues is important: career-arc volatility is driven by talent-pool size and structural support (prize money, development pipelines), both of which differ between the men's and women's tours.

det_09.label: Why readers care: the myth of sustained excellence
det_09.content: The reason this topic has audience pull beyond sports fandom is that it speaks to a broader intuition people carry about careers and success: that one great performance proves you belong, and you should be able to repeat it. The data say otherwise. Sustained excellence is rare; one-year breakouts without follow-up are not. That tension — between the narrative of 'you made it' and the statistics of 'most don't stay' — is what makes the one-hit wonder a perennial sports-writing topic. The Pudding's contribution is quantifying how many of these careers actually exist across three decades of pro sports, and naming them.

det_10.label: Caveats for the analyst
det_10.content: There are several things the analyst needs to watch for. First, a player who is currently active and only has one top-20 season so far may look like a one-hit wonder in the 2018 snapshot — but their career is unfinished; the dataset ends in 2017. Second, injuries, trades, and off-field events can manufacture a one-hit-wonder shape without it being 'just' regression. Third, the definition excludes players with fewer than five seasons — so cup-of-coffee rookies do not count. Fourth, sport-specific ranking stats make cross-sport comparison noisy: golf earnings are bottom-heavy and spiky (one win can rocket a player up the list), while basketball's VORP is smoother. The blog should report within-sport and also call out how the 'spike ratio' — peak-year rank divided by median rank — differs across leagues.

sources.title: One-Hit Wonders in Sports — The Pudding
facts: Minimum 5 seasons required; player careers starting after 1987 included

det_11.label: Benchmark: how rare is a true one-hit wonder?
det_11.content: Out of 1,130 players in the 30-year dataset, only a small fraction fit the strict definition of 'exactly one top-20 season, every other season outside the top 50.' A reasonable ballpark before the analyst runs numbers is that true one-hit wonders are on the order of 5–15% of ranked players per league — roughly one in ten careers. Having a rough prior lets the analyst frame findings: if they report that, say, 12% of NBA players meet the definition, that number can be contextualized against the reader's gut feeling that these stories 'feel rare.' They are rare — but not vanishingly so.
